```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE)
library(data.table)
a <- 'docs/assets/isolaser_permutation'
grid <- fread(file.path(a, 'grid_estimates.tsv'))
pick <- fread(file.path(a, 'selected_cutoffs.tsv'))
selected <- fread(file.path(a, 'selected_cutoff_associations.tsv'))
focus <- fread(file.path(a, 'focus_associations.tsv'))
row_summary <- fread(file.path(a, 'row_pvalue_summary.tsv'))
all_rows <- fread(file.path(a, 'row_pvalues.tsv'), na.strings=c('NA','nan','NaN',''))
batches <- fread(file.path(a, 'batches.tsv'))
fmt <- function(x) format(x, big.mark=',', trim=TRUE, scientific=FALSE)
pct <- function(x) sprintf('%.1f%%', 100*x)
stopifnot(nrow(grid)==32L, nrow(pick)==4L,
          all(c('selection','validation','focus') %in% batches$batch),
          all(pick$validation_meets_target),
          sum(!is.na(all_rows$ami)) == row_summary$tested_rows)
base <- grid[grepl('\\|dPSI\\|>=0.10, het>=1, row p<=any', cutoff)]
row5 <- grid[id == pick[level=='rows' & target==0.05, id]]
row10 <- grid[id == pick[level=='rows' & target==0.10, id]]
gene5 <- grid[id == pick[level=='genes' & target==0.05, id]]
gene10 <- grid[id == pick[level=='genes' & target==0.10, id]]
h <- focus[gene=='HNRNPK']
```

**The association-level answer:** the analysis has a permutation p-value and a
Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) adjusted q-value for each of
`r fmt(row_summary$tested_rows)` testable variant–exonic-part associations on
chr9 at 6 hours. **None has q < 0.05** with the current 2,000 full-dataset
permutations. The highlighted HNRNPK association has p =
`r sprintf('%.6f',h$p_conservative)` and q = `r sprintf('%.3f',h$q_bh)`.
Its separate 100,000-permutation p-value is more precise but is **unadjusted**.

For context, on chromosome 9 at 6 hours after stimulation,
`r base$obs_rows` variant–exonic-part associations passed the original 30-read
screen. A shuffled dataset had about `r sprintf('%.1f',base$val_null_rows)` such
rows on average. This suggests that the screen includes a real signal above the
background expected when allele labels are unrelated to splicing, but the
original screen is too permissive for a short list of confident examples.
A stricter cutoff retained **`r row5$obs_rows` rows from 3 genes**, with an
estimated null/observed ratio of **`r pct(row5$val_fdr_rows)`** in an independent
set of permutations. This is a *pilot result for chr9 at 6 hours*, not a
stimulation-response test or a genome-wide error rate.

# Adjusted p-value for each association

**The test:** for one variant–part association, compare its observed isoLASER
association score (AMI) with its own scores from the shuffled reads. A larger
AMI means a stronger allele–splicing link. If \(B\) permutations are run,

\[
p_{\mathrm{perm}} =
\frac{1 + \#\{\text{permuted AMI} \geq \text{observed AMI}\}}{B+1}.
\]

For the two full batches together, \(B=2{,}000\). A permutation with an
undefined score is counted as at least as extreme, making the reported p-value
conservative. With no permutation more extreme, the smallest available
p-value is \(1/2{,}001 \approx 0.00050\), not zero.

We apply the **BH multiple-testing adjustment** to these p-values across all
`r fmt(row_summary$tested_rows)` chr9, 6-hour rows with a defined observed
score. This yields one **q-value per association**. Smaller q-values offer
stronger evidence after accounting for the number tested. Here
**`r sum(all_rows$q_bh < 0.05, na.rm=TRUE)` rows have q < 0.05**, and
`r sum(all_rows$q_bh < 0.10, na.rm=TRUE)` have q < 0.10. Among the
`r row_summary$website_passing` original-screen rows,
`r row_summary$passing_with_q_lt_0.10` have q < 0.10. These are adjustments
**within chr9 at 6 hours**; including the other chromosomes and timepoints
will increase the number of tests.

Search the table by gene or variant. One row is one variant × exonic-part
association; several rows can involve the same gene. The **permutation p**
and **BH q** columns answer the association-level question. The table includes
every row with a defined observed score, including rows that did not pass the
separate original screening filters.

```{r association-q-table}
tested <- all_rows[!is.na(ami)]
tested[, Gene := sub('^[^_]*_', '', Gene_name)]
setorder(tested, q_bh, p_conservative, Gene)
qtab <- data.frame(Gene=tested$Gene, Variant=tested$variant_qual,
  `Exonic part`=tested$exonic_part, `Het donors`=tested$n_het,
  `ΔPSI`=tested$dpsi, `Permutation p`=tested$p_conservative,
  `BH q`=tested$q_bh, `Passed original screen`=tested$pass_website,
  check.names=FALSE)
DT::datatable(qtab, rownames=FALSE,
  options=list(pageLength=10, scrollX=TRUE, order=list(list(6,'asc')))) |>
  DT::formatSignif(columns=c('Permutation p','BH q'),digits=4)
```

[Download all rows, including those without a defined score](assets/isolaser_permutation/row_pvalues.tsv).
The recorded p-values follow the nonzero permutation convention described by
[Phipson and Smyth](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21044043/); the adjustment
uses the [Benjamini–Hochberg procedure](https://rss.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x).
The q-values are conditional on this read-shuffling null and should not be
interpreted as validated genome-wide q-values.

To obtain a **genome-wide adjusted q-value for every association**, run the
permutation analysis for the other chromosomes and timepoints, calculate a
permutation p-value for each test, then apply BH to the complete test family.
More full-dataset permutations would improve resolution for the strongest
rows. The focused HNRNPK run alone cannot supply a refined q-value for every
association.

# The question the permutation asks

isoLASER links a variant's allele to whether a long read includes an exonic part.
For each variant–part pair, a 2 × 2 table counts reads with the reference or
alternate allele and with the part included or excluded. A strong link can be
called `cis`, but screening many such tables can still produce apparent links
by chance. We ask: **how many would pass the same screen if we broke the
allele–splicing link while keeping the observed reads and their splicing
patterns?**

Here is a **made-up example**. H1 carries REF and H2 carries ALT for this variant.
The column “part included?” stays attached to each read during permutation.

| Read | Part included? | Original haplotype / allele | Shuffled haplotype / allele |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| A | Yes | H1 / REF | H2 / ALT |
| B | Yes | H1 / REF | H1 / REF |
| C | No | H2 / ALT | H1 / REF |
| D | No | H2 / ALT | H2 / ALT |

Originally, both inclusion reads carry REF and both exclusion reads carry ALT.
After one shuffle, each splicing outcome has one of each. Repeating the shuffle
shows how often a link at least as strong as the observed one appears by chance.

**The actual shuffle works within each donor × gene × phasing group.** It
redistributes haplotype labels among reads in that group. When a read changes
label, its alleles at the linked variants are flipped together; its exonic-part
statuses do not change. For reads without a usable haplotype label, alleles
are shuffled within that variant. The same shuffled allele is used for that
read across every part tested for the variant. Variant coverage and the donor
set selected from the *observed* data stay fixed. A shuffled table can have an
undefined score if too few reads remain on one allele; the cutoff analysis
treats it as failing the screen.

This preserves connections among parts and linked variants better than filling
each 2 × 2 table with independent random numbers. Its interpretation still
rests on reads being exchangeable within the groups where labels are shuffled;
it does not remove mapping bias or alignment artifacts.

# What we ran and checked

This first run covers **chr9, 6 hours, four donors** (CD_21, CD_31, CD_36,
CD_48). It was chosen because the HNRNPK example is on chr9. The original
screen required at least **30 informative reads from each contributing donor**
for a variant–part pair, an observed allele fraction of 0.25–0.75 for that
donor, a `cis` label, |ΔPSI| ≥ 0.10, a part at least 10 bp long, and no other
tested variant within 30 bp. A “passing row” means one
**variant × exonic part × timepoint association**; several rows can belong to
the same gene.

isoLASER did not save its variant-specific allele assignment for each read.
We therefore reran its Nanopore-model analysis once with a recording copy that
saved those assignments. The rerun, rather than the earlier unseeded output,
is the observed dataset used below. No alignment or variant calling is repeated
for each shuffle.

Before permuting, all four donors passed checks that the recording copy and a
control copy produce identical variant, splicing-table and haplotype outputs.
Every recorded variant–part read table reproduced isoLASER's counts. Pooling
and rescoring the unshuffled records then matched all **5,578 / 5,578** joint
rows from the rerun. This is a check that the permutation starts from the same
statistics as the observed analysis.

We ran **1,000 selection permutations**, then **1,000 independent validation
permutations** with a different random seed. A fixed grid of 32 cutoffs varies
|ΔPSI|, the minimum number of heterozygous donors (one or two), and each
row's empirical permutation p-value. The selection batch chooses a cutoff;
the validation batch estimates its null count again. A separate **100,000
permutation focus run** tests the selected HNRNPK association. The first,
older 1,000-permutation experiment is excluded from these results.

# How to read the screen-level result

For any cutoff, both real and shuffled datasets must pass **the same rules**.
The reported estimate is

\[
\text{estimated null/observed ratio}
= \frac{\text{mean number passing in a permuted dataset}}
       {\text{number passing in the observed dataset}}.
\]

For example, at the original cutoff, `r base$obs_rows` rows pass in the real
data and `r sprintf('%.3f',base$val_null_rows)` pass in a validation shuffle
on average: `r sprintf('%.3f',base$val_null_rows)` / `r base$obs_rows` =
**`r pct(base$val_fdr_rows)`**. This ratio is an *estimated permutation FDR*
under this shuffle scheme, not a guarantee that this exact fraction of the
observed rows is false.

```{r headline}
show <- rbindlist(list(
  data.table(Screen='Original website screen', Observed_rows=base$obs_rows,
             Null_rows=base$val_null_rows, Row_ratio=base$val_fdr_rows,
             Observed_genes=base$obs_genes, Null_genes=base$val_null_genes,
             Gene_ratio=base$val_fdr_genes),
  data.table(Screen='Selected 5% row cutoff', Observed_rows=row5$obs_rows,
             Null_rows=row5$val_null_rows, Row_ratio=row5$val_fdr_rows,
             Observed_genes=row5$obs_genes, Null_genes=row5$val_null_genes,
             Gene_ratio=row5$val_fdr_genes),
  data.table(Screen='Selected 10% row cutoff', Observed_rows=row10$obs_rows,
             Null_rows=row10$val_null_rows, Row_ratio=row10$val_fdr_rows,
             Observed_genes=row10$obs_genes, Null_genes=row10$val_null_genes,
             Gene_ratio=row10$val_fdr_genes)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(Screen=show$Screen, `Real rows`=show$Observed_rows,
  `Mean null rows`=sprintf('%.3f',show$Null_rows), `Row ratio`=pct(show$Row_ratio),
  `Real genes`=show$Observed_genes, `Mean null genes`=sprintf('%.3f',show$Null_genes),
  `Gene ratio`=pct(show$Gene_ratio), check.names=FALSE),row.names=FALSE)
```

The two ratios differ because two HNRNPK rows count as **two row signals but
one gene**. Counts per permutation are small, so the estimate is uncertain:
under the original rule, the central 95% of selection permutations had
`r base$sel_null_rows_95` passing rows. Gene-level ratios answer how many
genes appear under the null; a row-level cutoff is selected against the row
ratio.

![Number of passing rows in each selection permutation at the original screen cutoff; orange line shows the observed count.](assets/isolaser_permutation/null_passing_rows.png)

Among permuted rows with a defined association score, the `cis` label occurred
in **0.94%** of selection rows and **0.95%** of validation rows. That is close
to isoLASER's nominal 1% null-tail criterion and is a useful calibration
check for this dataset. It does not by itself validate every individual call.

# Which genes remain with stricter cutoffs?

The grid chose the cutoff retaining the most observed rows or genes while
meeting the chosen 5% or 10% **selection-batch** target. All four selected
cutoffs also met their target in the independent validation batch. The row
and gene targets are separate choices, so their lists need not be identical.

```{r chosen}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Target`=c('5% of rows','10% of rows','5% of genes','10% of genes'),
  `Additional rules`=c('≥2 donors; |ΔPSI| ≥0.10; row p ≤0.001',
                       '≥1 donor; |ΔPSI| ≥0.10; row p ≤0.001',
                       '≥1 donor; |ΔPSI| ≥0.20; row p ≤0.001',
                       '≥1 donor; |ΔPSI| ≥0.20; row p ≤0.003'),
  `Observed`=c(pick[level=='rows' & target==0.05, observed],
               pick[level=='rows' & target==0.10, observed],
               pick[level=='genes' & target==0.05, observed],
               pick[level=='genes' & target==0.10, observed]),
  `Validation ratio`=pct(c(row5$val_fdr_rows,row10$val_fdr_rows,gene5$val_fdr_genes,gene10$val_fdr_genes)),
  check.names=FALSE),row.names=FALSE)
```

At the **5% row target**, the four associations are two HNRNPK variant–part
rows, one XPA row, and one SMC2 row. At the **5% gene target**, ZDHHC21 also
appears, but its association has only one qualifying donor. C9orf72 appears
at the 10% gene target, also with one donor. These are association candidates;
this single timepoint does not show that stimulation changes their splicing.

```{r selected-rows}
z <- selected[level=='rows' & target==0.05]
knitr::kable(data.frame(Gene=z$gene, Variant=z$variant_qual,
  `Exonic part`=z$exonic_part, `Het donors`=z$n_het,
  `Pooled reads`=z$het_cov, `ΔPSI`=sprintf('%.3f',z$dpsi),
  check.names=FALSE),row.names=FALSE)
```

# HNRNPK: a focused check

The highlighted HNRNPK association links `r h$variant_qual` to
`r h$exonic_part`, with `r h$n_het` qualifying donors and
`r h$het_cov` pooled informative reads. Its observed |ΔPSI| is
`r sprintf('%.3f',abs(h$dpsi))`. None of the `r fmt(h$focus_perms)` focused
shuffles produced an association score at least as large, giving
\((0+1)/(100{,}000+1)\) = **`r sprintf('%.5f',h$focus_p_unadjusted)`**.
This is an *unadjusted, candidate-specific p-value* for this association,
selected after the initial screen. It is evidence that this particular link
is stronger than expected under the shuffle; it does not test a change from
0 to 6 hours or by itself control for the many associations screened.

Across all `r fmt(row_summary$tested_rows)` rows with a defined observed score,
the two full batches give **zero** BH q-values below 0.05 and
`r row_summary$passing_with_q_lt_0.10` original-screen rows below 0.10.
The HNRNPK row's BH q-value from those full batches is
`r sprintf('%.3f',h$q_bh)`. The 100,000 focused shuffles improve resolution
for HNRNPK's own p-value; they are not incorporated into that adjustment
across the chr9, 6-hour tested rows.

# Does this result make sense, and what remains?

Yes, with limits. The original screen retains more rows than the null average
(`r base$obs_rows` versus `r sprintf('%.1f',base$val_null_rows)`), while a
cutoff requiring stronger evidence retains fewer rows and has a much smaller
null/observed ratio. The independent validation batch gives a similar answer
to the selection batch (`r pct(row5$sel_fdr_rows)` versus
`r pct(row5$val_fdr_rows)` for the selected 5% row cutoff). The near-1% `cis`
rate among shuffled defined scores is also reassuring.

The null can miss technical artifacts that cause a real read-level
allele–splicing link, including allele-dependent mapping or variants close to
splice boundaries. Even the stringent four-row result merits read-alignment
inspection and independent support. Most importantly, this pilot covers
**only chr9 at 6 hours**. Repeating it across chromosomes and timepoints is
needed before reporting a genome-wide error rate or testing a stimulation
interaction. A change in which timepoints pass a cutoff is not, by itself,
a test of that interaction.
